subject: english-language-and-literature
title: English Language and Literature MYP 5 eAssessment Structure Mock (3 tasks, 80 marks)

questions.content:
[[Q 1.1 | A 2]]
Task 1: Analysing
Questions 1.1 to 1.4 focus on the key concept of communication. Question 1.5 focuses on the key concept of connections. The criteria assessed are A (Analysing) and B (Organizing). Suggested time for Questions 1.1 to 1.4: 15 minutes. Suggested time for Question 1.5: 35 minutes.

Text A: 'The Last Ferry Home' (an extract from a short story, written for this paper)
This extract describes a girl, Imara, waiting on a rain-soaked pier for her grandfather after the harbour has been closed by a storm.

By six o'clock the sea had turned the colour of old pewter. Imara stood at the end of the pier with her collar up, watching the lights of the mainland blink and vanish behind the swell. The harbour master had already chained the gate. "Nothing's crossing tonight, love," he had said, not unkindly, but she had stayed anyway.

Behind her the fish stalls were shuttered, their striped awnings snapping like flags in surrender. A single gull hung above the water, wings locked, going nowhere against the wind. She understood it perfectly.

Her grandfather had promised he would be on the last ferry. He had promised it on the telephone, in the slow, careful English he used when he wanted to be believed. "Wait for me by the lamp," he had said. So she waited by the lamp, and the lamp swung and buzzed, and its yellow circle shrank and grew on the wet boards like a pulse.

At seven, a bell began to toll somewhere out in the dark. Imara's heart lifted, then fell. It was only a buoy, rocking, ringing for no one.

She took out the small brass compass he had given her last winter and held it flat on her palm. The needle shivered, then settled, pointing steadily at the place where the lights had been. "Even when you can't see the way," he used to say, "you can know the direction." She closed her fingers around it. The rain ran down her wrists. She did not move from the lamp.

Text B: transcript of 'Keep Rowing', a two-minute public-awareness film about a community lifeboat crew (written for this paper; in the live exam this would be a video)
[Visual: a small orange lifeboat rides a grey swell. Slow, low piano music. The camera is placed at water level.]
Narrator (calm, quiet): "Nobody here is a hero. They're bakers and teachers and bus drivers."
[Visual: close-up of hands tightening a rope; cut to a clock on a wall showing 3.12 a.m.]
Narrator: "When the pager goes, they go. They don't ask who is out there. They only ask how fast."
[Visual: a wave breaks over the bow; the music stops completely for three seconds. Only wind.]
Narrator: "Courage isn't the absence of fear. It's what you do with the fear in your hands."
[Visual: the crew hauls a stranger aboard and wraps a blanket round them. The piano returns, warmer. Sunrise breaks over the water.]
On-screen text, white capitals on black: THEY KEEP ROWING SO OTHERS CAN COME HOME. Volunteer today.

Q 1.1 Comment on the use of weather in the opening of Text A. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 2 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies a use of weather with reference to the text but does not justify with examples or explanation, e.g. the sea is described as pewter-coloured. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): comments on a use of weather with some example and explanation, e.g. the 'old pewter' sea and the storm create a bleak, threatening mood that foreshadows disappointment for Imara. [1] Award 0 for no or incorrect reference to the text.

questions.content:
[[Q 1.2 | A 3]]
Refer to Text A (printed in Question 1.1). Explain the effect of the line: 'A single gull hung above the water, wings locked, going nowhere against the wind. She understood it perfectly.' (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 3 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies an effect without developing it, e.g. the line shows Imara is stuck. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): describes an effect with some example or explanation, e.g. the gull mirrors Imara: both are held in place by forces they cannot beat. [1] Level 3 (3 marks): explains an effect consistently with well-chosen quotation, e.g. the short sentence 'She understood it perfectly' links Imara to the gull, so the reader feels her helplessness and determination to stay, and 'locked' and 'going nowhere' suggest effort that gets no reward. [1]

questions.content:
[[Q 1.3 | A 2]]
Refer to Text B (printed in Question 1.1). Describe the purpose of the music in the film. (2 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 2 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies a purpose without explanation, e.g. the music sets the mood. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): describes a purpose with an example, e.g. the quiet piano creates a calm, respectful tone, then stops for three seconds during the wave so the silence shows danger, and returns warmer at sunrise to signal relief and hope. [1]

questions.content:
[[Q 1.4 | A 3]]
Refer to Text B (printed in Question 1.1). Analyse the effect of a technique used in the film. (3 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A, 3 marks. Level 1 (1 mark): identifies a technique and an effect with no development, e.g. a close-up shows the hands. [1] Level 2 (2 marks): describes the effect of one technique with some justification, e.g. the low camera at water level makes the audience feel inside the waves and so more aware of the risk. [1] Level 3 (3 marks): analyses the effect consistently with a precise example, e.g. the cut from the hands on the rope to the clock at 3.12 a.m. shows the crew act at the worst hour, so the audience admires their selflessness; the on-screen text 'KEEP ROWING SO OTHERS CAN COME HOME' ends with a direct call to action that turns admiration into support. [1] Accept any valid technique: narration, camera angle, silence, colour, contrast of sound.

questions.content:
[[Q 1.5 | A 10 | B 10]]
Refer to Text A and Text B (printed in Question 1.1). Compare and contrast how the concept of perseverance is explored in the two texts. (Approximately 350 words) (20 marks)

Criterion A (Analysing) is worth 10 marks and Criterion B (Organizing) is worth 10 marks.
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion A (10 marks) and Criterion B (10 marks), 20 marks in total. Criterion A: 9 to 10 marks for effective, perceptive analysis of content, language, structure and technique in BOTH texts with extensive well-chosen evidence; 6 to 8 for considerable analysis with sufficient evidence; 3 to 5 for adequate analysis with some evidence; 1 to 2 for limited analysis with few examples. Indicative content: Text A shows quiet, solitary perseverance through the lamp, the compass and the 'going nowhere' gull; sentence rhythm slows and the ending does not resolve. Text B shows collective, active perseverance through the crew, the clock and the 'keep rowing' slogan; music and camera shape admiration and a call to action. Contrast: individual and passive waiting versus group and active effort; hope held privately versus perseverance used to persuade an audience. Award up to [10] for Criterion A. Criterion B: 9 to 10 marks for effective organisation with a clear structure, comparison and contrast sustained throughout, effective linking and a conclusion; 6 to 8 for a considerable degree; 3 to 5 for an adequate degree with some comparison; 1 to 2 for limited, mostly separate treatment of each text. Award up to [10] for Criterion B.

questions.content:
[[Q 2.1 | C 10 | D 10]]
Task 2: Producing literary text
This task focuses on the key concept of creativity. The criteria assessed are C (Producing text) and D (Using language).

Image 1 (described in words): a shelf in a junk shop crowded with chipped teapots, clocks that have stopped, brass keys and one old pair of binoculars, all under a film of dust and lit by a thin beam of sunlight.
Image 2 (described in words): two glowing glass flasks, one green and one red, on a stone bench in a dark workshop, with three students leaning in to watch the liquids.

Using one of the images, write a scene in a science fiction story in which a character discovers an object's power. You may consider purpose, characterisation, setting, mood and point of view. State which image you are using before you start. (Approximately 350 words) (20 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion C (10 marks): 9 to 10 high degree of insight and imagination, perceptive stylistic choices, extensive precise detail; 6 to 8 considerable insight, thoughtful choices, sufficient detail; 3 to 5 some insight, some stylistic choices, some detail; 1 to 2 limited. A response that uses neither image nor the prompt scores 0 for C. Award up to [10] for Criterion C. Criterion D (10 marks): 9 to 10 effective range of vocabulary and sentence structures, consistently purposeful register, high accuracy with minor errors; 6 to 8 varied range, considerable accuracy, errors do not hinder communication; 3 to 5 adequate range, a degree of accuracy, errors sometimes hinder; 1 to 2 limited range, errors often hinder. Award up to [10] for Criterion D. Indicative content: a clear named image, a character who discovers and tests the power, rising tension, sensory description and a controlled ending.

questions.content:
[[Q 3.1 | B 10 | C 10 | D 10]]
Task 3: Producing non-literary text
This task focuses on the key concept of perspective. You will create a piece of non-literary writing in relation to the global context globalization and sustainability: sustainable development and resources. The criteria assessed are B (Organizing), C (Producing text) and D (Using language).

Write a speech for a school assembly on why reducing food waste matters for your community now and for future generations. Use a clear structure and persuasive techniques suited to a speech. (Approximately 350 words) (30 marks)
questions.mark_scheme: Criterion B (10 marks): organisation suited to a speech: a purposeful opening, three developed points, a persuasive close and the conventions of the text type (direct address, rhetorical devices); 9 to 10 effective, 6 to 8 considerable, 3 to 5 adequate, 1 to 2 limited. Award up to [10] for Criterion B. Criterion C (10 marks): perspective on the global context shown through insight, relevant detail and examples about waste, resources and future generations; 9 to 10 high degree of insight and extensive detail, 6 to 8 considerable, 3 to 5 some, 1 to 2 limited. Award up to [10] for Criterion C. Criterion D (10 marks): register suited to an assembly audience, varied sentence structures, persuasive techniques (rule of three, repetition, inclusive language, rhetorical questions), accurate grammar and punctuation; 9 to 10 high accuracy, 6 to 8 considerable, 3 to 5 a degree, 1 to 2 minimal. Award up to [10] for Criterion D.
